lesson.title: Pavlov's Bell: How We Learn by Association
lesson.summary: Classical conditioning is a form of learning in which a neutral stimulus, through repeated pairing with a stimulus that already produces a response, comes to produce a similar response on its own.
lesson.body:
Classical conditioning was discovered almost by accident. Ivan Pavlov, a Russian physiologist, was not originally studying learning at all; he was studying the digestive system of dogs, measuring how much they salivated in response to food. In the course of that research he noticed something that would end up being far more famous than his original digestion work: the dogs began salivating before the food ever appeared, in response to things reliably associated with feeding, like the sound of an assistant's footsteps. Rather than treating this as noise in his data, Pavlov redirected his research to understand it, and in doing so laid the foundation for one of the most important concepts in all of psychology.

Classical conditioning has a specific structure. It starts with an unconditioned stimulus, something that automatically and naturally produces a response without any learning required, food producing salivation, for example. That automatic reaction is called the unconditioned response. Separately, there is a neutral stimulus, something like a bell, that at first produces no particular reaction related to the response in question. When the neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with the unconditioned stimulus, presented just before or alongside it across many trials, the organism learns an association between the two. Eventually the previously neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus, capable of producing the response on its own, now called the conditioned response, even without the original unconditioned stimulus present.

What makes this form of learning distinct is that it is built entirely on association between two stimuli, rather than on consequences that follow a behavior, which is the basis of a different kind of learning covered elsewhere. Classical conditioning explains a great deal of everyday emotional and physiological learning that happens without any deliberate intention, from why a particular song can trigger a rush of feeling to why some people develop strong reactions, positive or negative, to smells, sounds, or places associated with important past experiences.

Pavlov's work is also a useful example of how psychology built itself into a rigorous, evidence based science. His careful, controlled, repeatable measurement of a physiological response gave early psychologists, including behaviorists like John Watson, a model for how to study behavior objectively rather than relying on introspection or speculation, which is part of why classical conditioning is often taught as a founding demonstration of the scientific method applied to the mind. The next three chapters take this same procedure apart piece by piece, looking closely at the unconditioned stimulus, the conditioned stimulus, and the conditioned response in turn.
